summary:
Article 629 of Ethiopia's 2004 Criminal Code makes same-sex conduct between men and between women a criminal offence. Prosecutions are uncommon, but the provision sustains stigma, harassment and violence against LGBTIQ+ people and produces near-total concealment of identity. Stakeholder submissions to the country's Universal Periodic Review put the maximum penalty at one year, with harsher terms available under aggravating provisions; a 2009 study of the same code reports up to three years for male homosexuality. The two accounts of the ceiling have not been reconciled.

No legal gender recognition mechanism exists. Neither a surgical nor a psychiatric pathway to changing legal sex is available, so trans men remain legally women and trans women legally men. A relationship that the law reads through birth-registered sex can therefore fall inside the prohibition on same-sex conduct, and a trans visitor travelling with a partner whose registered sex matches their own is exposed to the criminal law and not only to social disapproval.

Enforcement runs through public order and morality policing rather than through the courts. On 10 August 2023 security forces raided hospitality venues in Addis Ababa, shutting guest houses and arresting managers, after the city's Peace and Security Administration Bureau announced measures against hotels, restaurants, guest houses and other entertainment venues suspected of involvement in homosexual acts and called on the public to report such cases. The same month produced an online incitement campaign that ended in physical attacks.

Police conduct documented by ILGA World includes residential searches without warrants following complaints from neighbours and physical abuse during detention. In a 2014 case a detained man was refused legal counsel and assaulted by other inmates, and no trial record was found. In January 2021 police disclosed the sexual orientation of two people released from detention to their families, and one of them subsequently died by suicide. Activists report surveillance and entrapment, and the US State Department recorded harassment and violence rising toward the end of 2023.

The Charities and Societies Proclamation, Article 69, bars registration of LGBTI organisations as contrary to public morality, and groups operate without legal status. Pride events are not permitted and participants are not protected. A 2008 petition for equal rights signed by hundreds of gay people was blocked before reaching the prime minister's office, and a conference scheduled for Addis Ababa in 2012 was cancelled after religious groups denounced the organisers.

No hate-crime or hate-speech legislation covers gender identity, and there is no protection against arbitrary arrest on grounds of gender identity or expression. Workplace and housing discrimination protections do not extend to gender identity. The F&M Global Barometers series scores the country 'no' on every protection axis for each year from 2011 to 2024.

Discrimination is reported across education, employment and healthcare, and being identified as LGBTIQ+ carries a risk of physical violence and ostracism. Christian and Muslim bodies campaign for heavier penalties, and the Orthodox Church set out its position in June 2024. In March 2014 the Council of Ministers endorsed a bill that would have made homosexuality a non-pardonable offence, then cancelled both the bill and a planned anti-gay rally, with a government spokesman saying the existing jail term was sufficient.

Same-sex marriage has no legal recognition, and no mechanism recognises a trans person's partnership according to the partner's gender rather than registered sex. An unofficial ceremony held at a hotel in Addis Ababa in 2008 had no legal effect.

Stigma attached to HIV affects access to education, employment and community life. The AIDS Resource Center in Addis Ababa reported that most self-identified gay and lesbian callers, predominantly men, asked for help changing their behaviour to avoid discrimination, and many described anxiety, depression, identity crises and suicide attempts. Public claims blaming gay people for sexual violence against children and young men deter young people from seeking services. In December 2011 religious leaders tried to stop a sexual health seminar for men who have sex with men; the government intervened and the seminar went ahead at another location.

Document markers carry direct custodial risk. In July 2021 authorities in Germany ordered the deportation of a trans woman of Qatari origin who held Ethiopian citizenship. After someone discovered that her passport recorded her as male and attempted to extort her, she was reported to the Ethiopian authorities, held for about a year in a men's prison and subjected to physical and sexual abuse by staff and inmates. Officials in Germany argued that she would be safe because she could pass as cisgender, citing the absence of explicit law on gender identity.

In the early 2010s some media outlets, cooperating with the government, restricted discussion of what they termed LGBTQ ideology without any formal policy being enacted. Internet censorship has limited organising.
tangentialFactors:
Detention conditions shape what a criminal-law exposure actually means in practice. US State Department reporting on Ethiopia documents torture and harsh prison conditions alongside anti-terrorism prosecutions and restrictions on civil society under the charities and societies law, an environment in which a person held on a morality charge has little external scrutiny.

Historical and ethnographic material records a transgender woman in Nuer society, encountered by researcher Brian MacDermot, who received spiritual approval to change status and marry a husband, and homosexual relationships among shepherd boys of the Amhara and Qemant communities reported by David F. Greenberg. Neither has any bearing on the current statute.
localsOnly:
Residents who organise face the registration bar directly: LGBTI associations cannot obtain legal personality, which forecloses funding, premises and public programming, and leaves informal groups exposed. The DANA Social Club, founded in 2013 by Beki Abiy, campaigns for transgender people's access to sex reassignment surgery without legal standing.

Employment and housing protections do not cover gender identity, and dismissal or eviction on the basis of appearance or disclosure has no remedy. Healthcare settings carry the same exposure, with disclosure to providers risking wider circulation.

Police disclosure to family is a documented pattern rather than an isolated incident, and it places residents at risk inside their own households. The January 2021 case, in which one of two people whose orientation was revealed to relatives later died by suicide, is the recorded instance.

Religious mobilisation against LGBTIQ+ residents has been sustained: a December 2008 resolution by leaders of the Muslim, Orthodox, Protestant and Catholic communities urged lawmakers to write the prohibition into the constitution, and the 2014 anti-gay rally planned for 26 April by the Addis Ababa Youth Forum with a church-linked group was cancelled by the government alongside the non-pardonable offences bill.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty ceiling is unresolved. Stakeholder UPR submissions state one year with aggravating provisions; the 2009 Lund thesis states up to three years for male homosexuality. No text of Article 629 or sentencing record was available to settle the question.

Whether the provision is applied to women in practice is not established. The 2009 thesis describes female homosexuality as overlooked, and no reported prosecution of women was located.

No trans-specific violence series with a usable denominator was found, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made and no rate is reported here.

Ethiopian airport and border screening practice for trans travellers is not sourced beyond the passport-marker case described above; whether secondary screening or document flagging occurs at entry is unknown.

The outcome of the 2021 deportation case after arrival in Ethiopia is not documented in the available sources.
